rules.title: The cramfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The cramfs filesystem is a compressed, read-only filesystem intended for systems with limited memory. A cramfs image can be mounted and used without first decompressing the image.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling cramfs when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The freevxfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The freevxfs filesystem is a free implementation of the Veritas filesystem and is the primary filesystem type used on HP-UX systems.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling freevxfs when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The hfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The hfs filesystem is a hierarchical filesystem that allows Macintosh (Mac OS) volumes to be mounted on Linux.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling hfs when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The hfsplus kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The hfsplus filesystem is a hierarchical filesystem designed to succeed hfs, enabling Macintosh (Mac OS) volumes to be mounted on Linux.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling hfsplus when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The jffs2 kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The jffs2 (Journaling Flash File System 2) filesystem is a journaling filesystem designed for use on flash memory devices.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling jffs2 when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The overlayfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: OverlayFS provides a union-mount filesystem that combines an upper and lower filesystem into a single unified view. It is commonly used by container runtimes such as Docker and Podman.
rules.impact: The overlayfs module has known privilege-escalation vulnerabilities, including CVE-2021-3493 and CVE-2023-0386. Disabling unused OverlayFS support reduces the local attack surface.

rules.title: The squashfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The squashfs filesystem is a compressed, read-only filesystem often used for LiveCD and similar images. A squashfs image can be mounted without first decompressing it.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling squashfs when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The usb-storage kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The usb-storage kernel module enables the system to use USB mass-storage devices such as flash drives and external disks.
rules.impact: Restricting USB storage reduces the risk that removable media will be used to exfiltrate data, introduce malware, or bypass local security controls.

rules.title: /tmp is a separate partition
rules.explanation: The /tmp directory is a world-writable location used for temporary files. Placing it on a dedicated partition or tmpfs enables restrictive mount options and isolates temporary storage from the root filesystem.
rules.impact: Isolating /tmp limits the impact of disk-space exhaustion through temporary files and allows protective mount options that harden a frequently abused writable location.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /tmp
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /tmp is world-writable, applying nodev stops users from creating device nodes there that could be used to access hardware or bypass device-access controls.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /tmp
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /tmp is world-writable, applying nosuid prevents placement of setuid binaries that could be used for privilege escalation.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /tmp
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /tmp is world-writable, applying noexec reduces the risk that uploaded or staged binaries will be executed directly from temporary storage.

rules.title: /dev/shm is a separate partition
rules.explanation: /dev/shm is a shared-memory filesystem (typically tmpfs) used for inter-process communication. Mounting it separately enables restrictive mount options.
rules.impact: Isolating /dev/shm allows protective mount options that reduce abuse of shared memory as a staging area for malicious code or privilege-escalation artifacts.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /dev/shm
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nodev on /dev/shm prevents creation of device nodes in shared memory that could bypass device-access controls.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /dev/shm
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nosuid on /dev/shm prevents setuid binaries from being executed from shared memory for privilege escalation.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /dev/shm
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying noexec on /dev/shm reduces the risk that shared memory will be used as an in-memory execution staging area for malicious code.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /home
rules.explanation: The /home directory holds user home directories and personal data. Placing it on a separate partition isolates user data from system files and supports quotas and protective mount options.
rules.impact: Isolating /home limits the impact of disk exhaustion by user data on the root filesystem and enables mount options that harden user-writable storage.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /home
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /home is intended for user files, applying nodev prevents users from creating device nodes that could be used to access hardware or bypass device-access controls.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /home
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /home is intended for user files, applying nosuid prevents users from creating setuid binaries in /home that could be used for privilege escalation.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var
rules.explanation: The /var directory stores variable data such as logs, caches, spools, and application state. Placing it on a separate partition isolates growth of that data from the root filesystem.
rules.impact: Isolating /var reduces the risk that log or cache growth will fill the root filesystem and disrupt system services.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /var
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nodev on /var prevents creation of device nodes in variable-data directories that could bypass device-access controls.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /var
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nosuid on /var prevents setuid binaries from being placed or executed under /var if write access is obtained through a compromised service.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/tmp
rules.explanation: /var/tmp provides temporary storage that persists across reboots. Placing it on a separate partition enables restrictive mount options while isolating that storage from the root filesystem.
rules.impact: Isolating /var/tmp limits persistence of attacker-controlled temporary files across reboots and allows protective mount options on this writable location.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /var/tmp
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nodev on /var/tmp prevents creation of device nodes in persistent temporary storage that could bypass device-access controls.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /var/tmp
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nosuid on /var/tmp prevents setuid binaries from persisting across reboots in temporary storage for privilege escalation.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /var/tmp
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying noexec on /var/tmp reduces the risk that persistent temporary storage will be used to stage and execute malicious binaries across reboots.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/log
rules.explanation: The /var/log directory stores system and application logs. Placing it on a separate partition isolates log growth from the root filesystem and helps preserve logging capacity.
rules.impact: Isolating /var/log reduces the risk that log growth will fill the root filesystem and disrupt services, and helps protect log availability for investigation.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /var/log
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nodev on /var/log prevents creation of device nodes in the log directory that could bypass device-access controls.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /var/log
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nosuid on /var/log prevents setuid binaries from being executed from the log directory if write access is obtained.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /var/log
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying noexec on /var/log ensures the log partition remains storage-only and reduces the risk of executing binaries planted in log directories.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: The /var/log/audit directory stores audit daemon logs. Placing it on a separate partition isolates audit storage from other log growth and supports compliance retention.
rules.impact: Isolating /var/log/audit helps preserve audit records when other logs grow rapidly and reduces the chance that audit capacity will be exhausted by unrelated logging.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nodev on /var/log/audit prevents creation of device nodes in audit log storage that could bypass device-access controls.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nosuid on /var/log/audit prevents setuid binaries from being executed from the audit log partition.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying noexec on /var/log/audit keeps the audit partition storage-only and reduces the risk of executing binaries planted among audit logs.

rules.title: AppArmor is installed
rules.explanation: AppArmor is a Mandatory Access Control (MAC) framework that confines programs according to security profiles enforced by the kernel. It is the standard MAC system on Ubuntu.
rules.impact: Without AppArmor, compromised applications are limited only by discretionary user permissions, increasing the impact of application-level compromise.

rules.title: AppArmor is enabled in the bootloader configuration
rules.explanation: AppArmor is enabled for early boot by passing kernel parameters such as apparmor=1 and security=apparmor through the bootloader configuration.
rules.impact: If AppArmor is not enabled at boot, confinement profiles are not applied during system startup, leaving processes unprotected until AppArmor is activated later.

rules.title: All AppArmor profiles are in enforce or complain mode
rules.explanation: Loaded AppArmor profiles should be active in either enforce mode (policy violations are blocked) or complain mode (violations are logged). Profiles that are unloaded or unconfined provide no confinement.
rules.impact: Inactive or unconfined profiles leave applications without MAC restrictions, increasing the impact of a compromised process.

rules.title: All AppArmor profiles are in enforce mode
rules.explanation: Enforce mode applies AppArmor policy by blocking unauthorized operations rather than only logging them. It is the recommended mode for production systems.
rules.impact: In complain mode, policy violations are logged but not prevented, so a compromised application can continue actions that violate its intended confinement.

rules.title: A bootloader password is set
rules.explanation: A GRUB bootloader password restricts unauthorized modification of boot parameters and menu entries before the operating system starts.
rules.impact: Without a bootloader password, an attacker with physical console access can alter boot parameters (for example to obtain a root shell) and bypass normal authentication.

rules.title: Access to the bootloader configuration is configured
rules.explanation: The GRUB configuration file contains boot parameters and may include password hashes. Restrictive ownership and mode limit who can read or modify that configuration.
rules.impact: World-readable bootloader configuration can expose password hashes for offline attack, while writable configuration allows unauthorized changes to boot behavior.

rules.title: Address space layout randomization (ASLR) is enabled
rules.explanation: Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) randomizes the locations of key process memory regions such as the stack, heap, and shared libraries. A value of 2 enables full randomization.
rules.impact: ASLR makes memory-corruption exploits such as buffer overflows and return-oriented programming significantly harder by reducing predictability of process address layouts.

rules.title: Ptrace_scope is restricted
rules.explanation: The kernel.yama.ptrace_scope setting restricts which processes may use ptrace to inspect or modify other processes.
rules.impact: Unrestricted ptrace allows an unprivileged process to attach to other user processes and read memory that may contain credentials, keys, or session tokens.

rules.title: Core dump creation is restricted
rules.explanation: Core dumps capture a process memory image at the time of a crash and may include passwords, keys, and other sensitive data. Restricting dump creation and access limits exposure of that content.
rules.impact: Unrestricted core dumps can leave readable memory images from privileged processes, enabling recovery of secrets after a crash or deliberate dump.

rules.title: Automatic error reporting is disabled
rules.explanation: Apport is Ubuntu's automatic crash-reporting service. It can collect crash data and send reports, which may include sensitive process information.
rules.impact: Automatic crash reporting may disclose sensitive data and adds an unnecessary service attack surface on hardened servers where outbound crash telemetry is not required.

rules.title: The message of the day is configured correctly
rules.explanation: The /etc/motd file displays a message after successful login. It should present an authorized-use notice and avoid disclosing detailed system or kernel version information.
rules.impact: Disclosing OS or kernel details in the MOTD aids reconnaissance and helps an attacker identify applicable exploits after obtaining a session.

rules.title: The local login warning banner is configured correctly
rules.explanation: The /etc/issue file is displayed before local login. It should contain an authorized-access warning and avoid technical details about the system.
rules.impact: System details in the local login banner provide reconnaissance information before authentication and can weaken the clarity of authorized-use notices.

rules.title: The remote login warning banner is configured correctly
rules.explanation: The /etc/issue.net file is displayed to remote users before login (for example via SSH). It should contain an authorized-access warning without disclosing OS type or version.
rules.impact: Remote banner disclosure of OS details assists reconnaissance before authentication and can undermine the legal and policy value of an authorized-use notice.

rules.title: Access to /etc/motd is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/motd file should be owned by root with mode 0644 or more restrictive so that unprivileged users cannot modify the post-login message.
rules.impact: Unauthorized modification of /etc/motd can be used for social engineering or to display misleading information to users after login.

rules.title: Access to /etc/issue is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/issue file should be owned by root with restrictive permissions so that unprivileged users cannot alter the local login banner.
rules.impact: Unauthorized modification of /etc/issue can present false warnings or solicit credentials before users authenticate.

rules.title: Access to /etc/issue.net is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/issue.net file should be owned by root with mode 0644 or more restrictive so that unprivileged users cannot alter the remote login banner.
rules.impact: Unauthorized modification of /etc/issue.net can present misleading or phishing content to users connecting remotely.

rules.title: GDM is removed
rules.explanation: GDM (GNOME Display Manager) provides graphical login. On servers that do not require a graphical console, GDM is unnecessary.
rules.impact: Removing unused display-manager software reduces the local attack surface associated with graphical sessions and related components.

rules.title: The GDM login banner is configured
rules.explanation: When GDM is used, the graphical login screen should display an authorized-access warning consistent with organizational policy.
rules.impact: A clear login banner supports policy enforcement and helps establish that only authorized use of the system is permitted.

rules.title: The GDM disable-user-list option is enabled
rules.explanation: The GDM disable-user-list setting hides account names on the graphical login screen so that valid usernames are not enumerated to casual observers.
rules.impact: Displaying a user list discloses account names and can focus password-guessing or social-engineering attacks on specific accounts.

rules.title: GDM screen lock is configured when the user is idle
rules.explanation: GDM/GNOME screen-lock settings automatically lock an idle graphical session, requiring re-authentication before further use.
rules.impact: An unlocked idle graphical session allows anyone with physical access to the console to continue working under the logged-in user's privileges.

rules.title: GDM screen lock settings cannot be overridden
rules.explanation: Locking screen-lock settings through dconf locks prevents users from changing idle-lock policy in their GNOME session.
rules.impact: If users can disable automatic screen lock, idle sessions may remain unprotected contrary to organizational security policy.

rules.title: Automatic mounting of removable media is disabled in GDM
rules.explanation: GDM/GNOME automount settings control whether removable media such as USB storage is mounted automatically when attached during a graphical session.
rules.impact: Automatic mounting of removable media increases the risk that untrusted devices will be attached and processed without deliberate administrator action.

rules.title: The GDM autorun-never setting is enabled
rules.explanation: The autorun-never setting prevents automatic execution of programs or content from removable media in the graphical desktop environment.
rules.impact: Disabling autorun reduces the risk that malicious removable media will trigger automatic execution of attacker-controlled code.

rules.title: The GDM autorun-never setting cannot be overridden
rules.explanation: Locking the autorun-never setting through dconf locks prevents users from re-enabling autorun behavior for removable media.
rules.impact: If users can re-enable autorun, organizational controls against automatic execution from removable media can be bypassed.

rules.title: XDMCP is not enabled
rules.explanation: XDMCP (X Display Manager Control Protocol) enables remote graphical display-manager access. It is an older protocol with weak security properties compared with modern remote-access methods.
rules.impact: Enabled XDMCP expands remote attack surface for graphical sessions and can expose display-manager services over the network without modern encryption and authentication.

rules.title: Autofs services are not in use
rules.explanation: autofs automatically mounts filesystems on demand when paths are accessed. It is used for on-demand mounting of local or network filesystems.
rules.impact: If on-demand automounting is not required, retaining autofs increases the attack surface and may allow unintended mounting of network or local resources.

rules.title: Avahi-daemon services are not in use
rules.explanation: Avahi implements mDNS/DNS-SD (Zeroconf) service discovery so hosts can advertise and discover services on the local network.
rules.impact: If Zeroconf discovery is not required, Avahi increases network exposure and can assist reconnaissance by advertising available services.

rules.title: DHCP server services are not in use
rules.explanation: A DHCP server assigns IP addressing and related network parameters to clients on a network segment.
rules.impact: An unintended DHCP server can distribute malicious gateways or DNS settings and disrupt or redirect client traffic.

rules.title: DNS server services are not in use
rules.explanation: A DNS server resolves hostnames to addresses for clients. Hosts that are not designated name servers should not run DNS server software.
rules.impact: An unintended DNS server expands the attack surface and may be abused for spoofing, cache poisoning, or covert DNS-based channels.

rules.title: Dnsmasq services are not in use
rules.explanation: dnsmasq is a lightweight service that can provide DNS caching, DNS forwarding, and DHCP functions on a host.
rules.impact: If the system is not intended to act as a DNS cache, DNS forwarder, or DHCP server, retaining dnsmasq increases the attack surface.

rules.title: FTP server services are not in use
rules.explanation: FTP servers provide file transfer using a protocol that transmits credentials and data without encryption.
rules.impact: If FTP service is not required, removing it eliminates cleartext credential exposure and reduces a historically vulnerability-prone network service.

rules.title: LDAP server services are not in use
rules.explanation: An LDAP server (such as slapd) provides directory services for authentication and organizational data.
rules.impact: If the host is not intended to provide directory services, retaining an LDAP server increases the attack surface around credential and directory data.

rules.title: Message access server services are not in use
rules.explanation: Message access servers such as IMAP and POP3 (for example Dovecot) provide remote access to stored email mailboxes.
rules.impact: If the host is not a mail server, retaining IMAP/POP3 services expands the network attack surface without providing required functionality.

rules.title: NFS services are not in use
rules.explanation: NFS (Network File System) allows remote clients to mount and access filesystems over the network.
rules.impact: If the host is not intended to export or serve NFS shares, retaining NFS services increases exposure of filesystem data and related RPC infrastructure.

rules.title: NIS server services are not in use
rules.explanation: NIS (Network Information Service) is a legacy directory service historically used to distribute account and configuration data across hosts.
rules.impact: NIS lacks modern encryption and authentication protections. Retaining it when unused exposes sensitive account data and expands legacy attack surface.

rules.title: Print server services are not in use
rules.explanation: CUPS provides printing services and related network print protocols. Hosts that do not provide printing typically do not require CUPS.
rules.impact: Unnecessary CUPS services expand the network attack surface. Print-stack vulnerabilities have included remote code execution risks.

rules.title: Rpcbind services are not in use
rules.explanation: rpcbind maps RPC program numbers to network ports and is used by RPC-based services such as NFS and NIS.
rules.impact: If RPC services are not required, retaining rpcbind discloses RPC service information and increases the attack surface of legacy RPC infrastructure.

rules.title: Rsync services are not in use
rules.explanation: The rsync daemon provides network file synchronization. In daemon mode it can expose filesystem paths according to its configuration.
rules.impact: If rsync daemon service is not required, retaining it increases the risk of unauthorized file access and expands network attack surface.

rules.title: Samba file server services are not in use
rules.explanation: Samba implements SMB/CIFS file and print sharing for interoperability with Windows and other SMB clients.
rules.impact: If SMB file sharing is not required, removing Samba reduces a substantial network attack surface commonly used for lateral movement.

rules.title: SNMP services are not in use
rules.explanation: SNMP is used for remote monitoring and management of systems and network devices. Older SNMP versions rely on weakly protected community strings.
rules.impact: If SNMP monitoring is not required, removing SNMP reduces exposure of system information and eliminates weakly authenticated management interfaces.

rules.title: TFTP server services are not in use
rules.explanation: TFTP provides simple file transfer without authentication and is commonly associated with network boot (PXE) environments.
rules.impact: If TFTP/PXE service is not required, retaining TFTP allows unauthenticated network read/write of configured paths and expands attack surface.

rules.title: Web proxy services are not in use
rules.explanation: Web proxies such as Squid forward and may cache HTTP/HTTPS client traffic between users and the Internet.
rules.impact: An unintended proxy can bypass organizational web controls and provide covert outbound connectivity for users or malware.

rules.title: Web server services are not in use
rules.explanation: Web servers such as Apache and Nginx serve HTTP/HTTPS content. Hosts that are not designated web servers should not run these services.
rules.impact: Unnecessary web servers expand the network attack surface and may expose internal content or web application vulnerabilities.

rules.title: Xinetd services are not in use
rules.explanation: xinetd is a super-server that listens for network requests and starts corresponding service programs on demand. Many services historically managed by xinetd are legacy protocols.
rules.impact: Retaining xinetd when unused increases the likelihood that insecure legacy network services will be exposed and expands overall network attack surface.

rules.title: X Window Server services are not in use
rules.explanation: An X Window System server provides graphical display services. Production servers typically do not require a local graphical environment.
rules.impact: Removing unused X Window System components reduces a complex local attack surface and avoids unnecessary graphical-session exposure on servers.

rules.title: The mail transfer agent is configured for local-only mode
rules.explanation: A mail transfer agent (MTA) such as Postfix relays and delivers email. Binding the MTA to localhost restricts it to local delivery rather than accepting network mail.
rules.impact: An MTA listening on external interfaces can be abused as an open relay and exposes mail-protocol attack surface on hosts that should only send local mail.

rules.title: The NIS client is not installed
rules.explanation: The NIS client retrieves account and configuration information from a NIS server over the network using a legacy, weakly protected protocol.
rules.impact: NIS client use can expose credential material on the network. Removing unused NIS clients reduces reliance on insecure legacy authentication infrastructure.

rules.title: The rsh client is not installed
rules.explanation: The rsh client executes remote commands using the legacy rsh protocol, which does not provide encryption of session data.
rules.impact: Presence of an rsh client increases the risk of cleartext remote command sessions. SSH provides a secure replacement for remote execution.

rules.title: The talk client is not installed
rules.explanation: The talk client is a legacy utility for interactive text messaging between users on networked systems.
rules.impact: Unused messaging clients add unnecessary software and may transmit messages without encryption. Removing them reduces local attack surface.

rules.title: The telnet client is not installed
rules.explanation: The telnet client provides remote terminal access using a protocol that transmits data, including credentials, without encryption.
rules.impact: Presence of a telnet client increases the likelihood of cleartext remote sessions. SSH is the preferred secure alternative.

rules.title: The LDAP client is not installed
rules.explanation: LDAP client utilities (such as ldap-utils) query directory services. Hosts that do not need to query LDAP typically do not require these tools.
rules.impact: Unused LDAP clients can facilitate reconnaissance of directory infrastructure if a host is compromised.

rules.title: The FTP client is not installed
rules.explanation: The FTP client transfers files using a protocol that transmits credentials and data without encryption.
rules.impact: Presence of an FTP client increases the risk of cleartext credential exposure during file transfer. SFTP or other encrypted methods are preferred.

rules.title: A single time synchronization daemon is in use
rules.explanation: Accurate system time is required for authentication protocols, certificate validation, and reliable log timestamps. Exactly one NTP/time-synchronization daemon should provide timekeeping.
rules.impact: Conflicting or absent time synchronization can break Kerberos and TLS validation and undermine forensic correlation of log events across systems.

rules.title: Systemd-timesyncd is configured with authorized time servers
rules.explanation: systemd-timesyncd synchronizes system time using configured NTP sources. Authorized organizational time servers should be specified when timesyncd is used.
rules.impact: Synchronization with unauthorized NTP sources can allow manipulation of system time, affecting authentication, logging, and certificate validity.

rules.title: Systemd-timesyncd is enabled and running
rules.explanation: When systemd-timesyncd is the selected time-synchronization client, it should be enabled at boot and actively running.
rules.impact: Without an active time client, system clocks drift, which can break Kerberos, TLS, and reliable security-event timestamps.

rules.title: Chrony is configured with authorized time servers
rules.explanation: Chrony synchronizes system time using NTP sources. The server and pool directives identify authorized time servers or pools.
rules.impact: Proper chrony configuration with authorized sources helps maintain accurate time for security protocols and consistent enterprise-wide log timestamps.

rules.title: Chrony runs as the _chrony user
rules.explanation: Chrony can drop privileges and run as the unprivileged _chrony user rather than remaining root for routine operation.
rules.impact: Running chronyd with least privilege limits the impact of a compromise of the time-synchronization daemon.

rules.title: Chrony is enabled and running
rules.explanation: When chrony is the selected time-synchronization client, chronyd should be enabled at boot and actively running.
rules.impact: A non-running chrony client allows clock drift that can disrupt authentication, certificate validation, and forensic log correlation.

rules.title: The cron daemon is enabled and active
rules.explanation: The cron daemon executes scheduled jobs for system maintenance and administrative tasks according to crontab schedules.
rules.impact: An inactive cron daemon may prevent timely execution of security-related maintenance such as log rotation and integrity checks.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/crontab are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/crontab file defines system-wide cron schedules. Restrictive ownership and mode limit who can read or modify those jobs.
rules.impact: Unauthorized write access to /etc/crontab can introduce jobs that run with elevated privileges, providing persistence or privilege abuse.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/cron.hourly are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.hourly directory contains scripts executed hourly by cron, typically with root privileges.
rules.impact: Unauthorized write access to /etc/cron.hourly can place scripts that run hourly as root, enabling persistence and privilege abuse.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/cron.daily are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.daily directory contains scripts executed daily by cron, typically with root privileges.
rules.impact: Unauthorized write access to /etc/cron.daily can place scripts that run daily as root, enabling persistence and privilege abuse.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/cron.weekly are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.weekly directory contains scripts executed weekly by cron, typically with root privileges.
rules.impact: Unauthorized write access to /etc/cron.weekly can place infrequently run root jobs that are harder to notice during routine monitoring.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/cron.monthly are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.monthly directory contains scripts executed monthly by cron, typically with root privileges.
rules.impact: Unauthorized write access to /etc/cron.monthly can place infrequently run root jobs that provide long-lived persistence.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/cron.d are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.d directory holds drop-in cron schedule files processed by the cron daemon.
rules.impact: Unauthorized write access to /etc/cron.d can introduce named cron jobs that execute with elevated privileges on an attacker-chosen schedule.

rules.title: Crontab is restricted to authorized users
rules.explanation: Access to user crontab can be controlled with /etc/cron.allow (allowlist) or /etc/cron.deny. An allowlist model restricts crontab use to explicitly authorized users.
rules.impact: Unrestricted crontab access allows any local user to schedule recurring jobs, increasing the impact of account compromise and complicating monitoring.

rules.title: At is restricted to authorized users
rules.explanation: The at utility schedules one-time job execution. Access can be controlled with /etc/at.allow (allowlist) or /etc/at.deny.
rules.impact: Unrestricted at access allows any local user to schedule arbitrary one-time commands, increasing the impact of account compromise.

rules.title: Wireless interfaces are disabled
rules.explanation: Wireless network interfaces provide connectivity outside wired network paths and perimeter controls typically applied to servers.
rules.impact: Active wireless interfaces on servers can bypass intended network segmentation and expose the host to adjacent wireless attackers.

rules.title: Bluetooth services are not in use
rules.explanation: Bluetooth services enable short-range wireless connectivity for peripherals and related profiles through stacks such as BlueZ.
rules.impact: If Bluetooth is not required, disabling it reduces a local wireless attack surface associated with historically serious Bluetooth vulnerabilities.

rules.title: The dccp kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: DCCP (Datagram Congestion Control Protocol) is a transport-layer protocol rarely required in typical server environments.
rules.impact: Unnecessary protocol support increases the local attack surface. Disabling the DCCP kernel module when DCCP is not required reduces that exposure.

rules.title: The tipc kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: TIPC (Transparent Inter-Process Communication) is a protocol used by some clustered applications for inter-node messaging.
rules.impact: Unnecessary protocol support increases the local attack surface. Disabling TIPC when cluster software does not require it reduces that exposure.

rules.title: The rds kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: RDS (Reliable Datagram Sockets) is a protocol used in some high-performance clustered environments.
rules.impact: Unnecessary protocol support increases the local attack surface. Disabling RDS when it is not required reduces that exposure.

rules.title: The sctp kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol) is a transport-layer protocol that supports message-oriented communication with multiple streams in a single association.
rules.impact: Unnecessary protocol support increases the local attack surface. Disabling the SCTP kernel module when SCTP is not required reduces that exposure.

rules.title: IP forwarding is disabled
rules.explanation: IP forwarding allows a host to route packets between network interfaces, effectively acting as a router.
rules.impact: On hosts that are not routers, enabling IP forwarding expands the ability to redirect traffic between segments after compromise.

rules.title: Packet redirect sending is disabled
rules.explanation: ICMP redirects inform other hosts of preferred routes. Sending redirects is normally a router function rather than a host function.
rules.impact: A host that sends ICMP redirects can influence routing decisions of other systems and contribute to traffic redirection attacks.

rules.title: Bogus ICMP responses are ignored
rules.explanation: Some ICMP error responses are considered bogus or unexpected for the local TCP/IP stack. Ignoring them reduces noise and misuse of malformed ICMP traffic.
rules.impact: Processing unexpected ICMP responses can aid network scanning and may contribute to amplification or topology disclosure.

rules.title: ICMP broadcast requests are ignored
rules.explanation: Responding to ICMP echo requests sent to broadcast addresses can allow a host to participate in Smurf-style reflected denial-of-service attacks.
rules.impact: Ignoring ICMP broadcast echoes prevents the host from amplifying attacker traffic toward third-party victims.

rules.title: ICMP redirects are not accepted
rules.explanation: ICMP redirects can update the kernel routing table based on messages from other hosts claiming a better route.
rules.impact: Accepting ICMP redirects from untrusted hosts enables route poisoning and can redirect traffic through attacker-controlled systems.

rules.title: Secure ICMP redirects are not accepted
rules.explanation: Secure ICMP redirects are redirects accepted only from a configured gateway. Even gateway-sourced redirects can alter host routing unexpectedly.
rules.impact: Accepting secure redirects still allows routing changes if a gateway is compromised or spoofed, supporting man-in-the-middle traffic redirection.

rules.title: Reverse path filtering is enabled
rules.explanation: Reverse path filtering drops packets whose source address is not reachable via the receiving interface, helping detect and block spoofed sources.
rules.impact: Without reverse path filtering, spoofed-source packets are more likely to be accepted, aiding ACL bypass and certain network attacks.

rules.title: Source-routed packets are not accepted
rules.explanation: IP source routing allows a sender to specify intermediate hops for a packet path. This legacy feature is rarely required on modern hosts.
rules.impact: Accepting source-routed packets can help attackers bypass intended routing and filtering controls.

rules.title: Suspicious packets are logged
rules.explanation: Logging martian and otherwise suspicious packets records traffic with impossible or unexpected source addresses for monitoring and investigation.
rules.impact: Without logging suspicious packets, spoofing attempts and related network anomalies are harder to detect and investigate.

rules.title: TCP SYN cookies are enabled
rules.explanation: TCP SYN cookies allow a server to validate new TCP connections under SYN flood conditions without retaining full connection state for every SYN.
rules.impact: Without SYN cookies, SYN flood attacks can exhaust incomplete-connection tables and deny new legitimate connections.

rules.title: IPv6 router advertisements are not accepted
rules.explanation: IPv6 Router Advertisements (RA) advertise default routers and prefixes used for address autoconfiguration on a link.
rules.impact: Accepting unsolicited RAs can allow attackers to inject rogue IPv6 routers and redirect traffic, including on hosts primarily using IPv4.

rules.title: A single firewall configuration utility is in use
rules.explanation: Host firewall policy may be managed by UFW, nftables, or iptables tooling. Using multiple managers concurrently can produce conflicting rulesets.
rules.impact: Conflicting firewall managers create unpredictable filtering behavior and can leave unintended gaps or block legitimate traffic.

rules.title: UFW is installed
rules.explanation: UFW (Uncomplicated Firewall) is Ubuntu's frontend for managing host firewall rules. Installation is required when UFW is the chosen firewall utility.
rules.impact: Without a host firewall utility, inbound network services lack a consistent local filtering policy and may be reachable more broadly than intended.

rules.title: Iptables-persistent is not installed with UFW
rules.explanation: iptables-persistent and UFW both manage persistence of iptables-based rules. Installing both can cause conflicting restore behavior at boot.
rules.impact: Conflicting persistence mechanisms can load incomplete or unexpected rules after reboot, weakening host firewall policy.

rules.title: The UFW service is enabled
rules.explanation: The UFW service applies configured firewall rules and should be enabled so filtering remains active across reboots.
rules.impact: A disabled UFW service means configured rules are not enforced, leaving network ports reachable according to default kernel networking behavior.

rules.title: UFW loopback traffic is configured
rules.explanation: UFW should allow traffic on the loopback interface required for local inter-process communication, while blocking spoofed loopback addresses arriving on other interfaces.
rules.impact: Incorrect loopback handling can break local services or allow spoofed 127.0.0.0/8 addresses to bypass intended access controls.

rules.title: UFW rules exist for all open ports
rules.explanation: Each listening network port should have a corresponding explicit UFW allow rule aligned with approved services.
rules.impact: Mismatch between listening ports and firewall rules indicates policy gaps that can leave services unintentionally exposed or unavailable.

rules.title: A default deny policy is set in UFW
rules.explanation: A default-deny (deny/reject incoming) UFW policy allows only traffic that matches explicit allow rules.
rules.impact: Without default deny, newly opened ports may become reachable immediately, amplifying the impact of service misconfiguration.

rules.title: Nftables is installed
rules.explanation: nftables is a Linux packet-filtering framework that defines tables, chains, and rules for host firewall policy.
rules.impact: When nftables is the chosen firewall backend, the packages must be present so filtering rules can be defined and enforced.

rules.title: UFW is uninstalled or disabled with nftables
rules.explanation: When nftables is the primary firewall, UFW should be removed or disabled so two managers do not compete for packet-filter configuration.
rules.impact: Running UFW alongside nftables can create conflicting rules and unpredictable filtering outcomes.

rules.title: An nftables table exists
rules.explanation: In nftables, a table is the container for chains and rules. At least one table is required before meaningful filtering policy can be applied.
rules.impact: Without a configured table, nftables cannot enforce host packet filtering for inbound or forwarded traffic.

rules.title: Base chains exist in nftables
rules.explanation: Base chains (such as input, forward, and output) attach nftables rules to Netfilter hooks that process actual packets.
rules.impact: Without base chains, traffic is not evaluated against firewall policy at the primary hook points.

rules.title: Loopback traffic is configured in nftables
rules.explanation: nftables should allow legitimate loopback traffic for local services and block spoofed loopback addresses received on non-loopback interfaces.
rules.impact: Missing loopback allows can break local communication under default-deny policy, while missing spoofing blocks enable loopback-address abuse.

rules.title: A default deny policy is set in nftables
rules.explanation: A default drop policy on nftables base chains blocks traffic that does not match an explicit accept rule.
rules.impact: Without default drop, newly exposed ports may be reachable by default, increasing the impact of unintended service exposure.

rules.title: The nftables service is enabled
rules.explanation: The nftables service loads and maintains firewall rules and should be enabled so policy persists across reboots.
rules.impact: If nftables is not enabled as a service, rules may not be restored after reboot, leaving the host temporarily unfiltered.

rules.title: Nftables rules are persistent
rules.explanation: nftables rules should be stored in configuration that is loaded at system start so runtime rules survive reboot.
rules.impact: Non-persistent rules create unprotected windows after reboot or maintenance until rules are reapplied manually.

rules.title: Iptables packages are installed
rules.explanation: The iptables packages provide tools and components needed when iptables is used as the host firewall stack.
rules.impact: Without iptables tooling, an iptables-based host firewall cannot be managed or verified effectively.

rules.title: Nftables is not enabled with iptables
rules.explanation: When iptables is the primary firewall approach, nftables should not also be actively managing conflicting policy.
rules.impact: Concurrent iptables and nftables management can produce unpredictable filtering because modern kernels may implement iptables via nftables backends.

rules.title: UFW is not enabled with iptables
rules.explanation: UFW manages iptables rules through its own interface. Using UFW together with direct iptables administration can overwrite or conflict with rules.
rules.impact: Dual management through UFW and raw iptables can create gaps or unintended blocks in host firewall policy.

rules.title: A default deny policy is set in iptables
rules.explanation: A default DROP policy on iptables INPUT and FORWARD chains ensures only explicitly allowed traffic is accepted.
rules.impact: Without default deny, listening services may be reachable without restriction, undermining the protective role of the host firewall.

rules.title: Loopback traffic is configured in iptables
rules.explanation: iptables loopback rules should permit local inter-process communication and block spoofed loopback addresses from external interfaces.
rules.impact: Incorrect loopback configuration can break local services under default-deny policy or enable loopback-address spoofing.

rules.title: Iptables rules exist for all open ports
rules.explanation: Each approved listening port should have a matching explicit iptables allow rule consistent with firewall policy.
rules.impact: Ports without corresponding allow rules may be unreachable under default deny, or unintentionally exposed if policy is incomplete.

rules.title: A default deny policy is set in ip6tables
rules.explanation: ip6tables applies packet filtering to IPv6 traffic independently of IPv4 iptables rules. A default DROP policy should apply to IPv6 as well.
rules.impact: Without IPv6 default deny, IPv6 paths may remain open even when IPv4 is filtered, allowing policy bypass via the IPv6 stack.

rules.title: Loopback traffic is configured in ip6tables
rules.explanation: ip6tables should allow legitimate IPv6 loopback (::1) traffic and block spoofed loopback addresses on other interfaces.
rules.impact: Missing IPv6 loopback rules can break local services using ::1 or allow IPv6 loopback-address spoofing.

rules.title: Ip6tables rules exist for all open ports
rules.explanation: IPv6 listening services should have explicit ip6tables allow rules corresponding to approved ports and protocols.
rules.impact: Services reachable over IPv6 without matching ip6tables rules may bypass an IPv4-only firewall policy.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/ssh/sshd_config are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/ssh/sshd_config file controls SSH daemon behavior, including authentication and access settings. Restrictive ownership and mode limit who can read or change that policy.
rules.impact: World-readable sshd_config can reveal detailed SSH hardening settings to unprivileged users, while writable configuration allows unauthorized weakening of remote-access controls.

rules.title: Permissions on SSH private host key files are configured
rules.explanation: SSH host private keys authenticate the server to clients. Restrictive ownership and mode (typically root-only read) protect those keys from theft.
rules.impact: Compromise of host private keys enables impersonation of the server and man-in-the-middle attacks against connecting clients.

rules.title: Permissions on SSH public host key files are configured
rules.explanation: SSH host public keys are distributed to clients for server identity verification. They should be owned by root and readable as appropriate, without being writable by unprivileged users.
rules.impact: Writable host public keys can be replaced, undermining client verification of server identity and facilitating man-in-the-middle attacks.

rules.title: SSH access is configured
rules.explanation: sshd directives such as AllowUsers, AllowGroups, DenyUsers, and DenyGroups restrict which accounts may authenticate over SSH.
rules.impact: Without explicit access restrictions, all local accounts—including service accounts—may accept SSH logins, expanding remote compromise paths.

rules.title: The SSH banner is configured
rules.explanation: The SSH Banner setting displays a message before authentication. It is typically used to present an authorized-access warning.
rules.impact: An authorized-access banner supports compliance expectations and clarifies that unauthorized use of the system is prohibited.

rules.title: SSH ciphers are configured
rules.explanation: The sshd Ciphers setting selects encryption algorithms used to protect SSH session confidentiality after key exchange.
rules.impact: Weak or legacy ciphers increase the risk that intercepted SSH traffic can be decrypted, exposing session contents and credentials.

rules.title: SSH ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax are configured
rules.explanation: ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax control how the SSH server detects and terminates idle or unresponsive client sessions through keepalive messages.
rules.impact: Sessions left open indefinitely consume resources and may be hijacked if a user leaves a connection unattended. Appropriate timeouts reduce that risk.

rules.title: SSH DisableForwarding is enabled
rules.explanation: DisableForwarding disables SSH forwarding features such as TCP port forwarding, X11 forwarding, and agent forwarding in a single control.
rules.impact: SSH forwarding can create covert tunnels that bypass network controls. Disabling unused forwarding reduces that attack surface on hardened servers.

rules.title: SSH GSSAPIAuthentication is disabled
rules.explanation: GSSAPIAuthentication enables Kerberos/GSSAPI-based SSH authentication. It is typically needed only in environments that use that infrastructure.
rules.impact: Leaving GSSAPI authentication enabled when Kerberos is unused adds complexity and unnecessary authentication attack surface.

rules.title: SSH HostbasedAuthentication is disabled
rules.explanation: HostbasedAuthentication trusts remote hosts based on host identity rather than verifying individual users with keys or passwords.
rules.impact: Host-based trust allows access from compromised trusted hosts without additional user authentication, weakening remote-access controls.

rules.title: SSH IgnoreRhosts is enabled
rules.explanation: IgnoreRhosts causes sshd to ignore .rhosts and .shosts files as authentication sources. Those legacy trust files are insecure by modern standards.
rules.impact: Honoring rhosts-style trust can permit passwordless access from listed hosts and is vulnerable to host spoofing or trust abuse.

rules.title: SSH key exchange algorithms are configured
rules.explanation: Key exchange (KEX) algorithms establish the shared session secrets used to protect an SSH connection.
rules.impact: Weak key-exchange algorithms increase the risk that session keys can be recovered and SSH traffic decrypted.

rules.title: SSH LoginGraceTime is configured
rules.explanation: LoginGraceTime limits how long an unauthenticated SSH connection may remain open while authentication is attempted.
rules.impact: Excessive grace time allows attackers to hold many incomplete connections, consuming resources and widening the window for slow guessing attacks.

rules.title: SSH LogLevel is configured
rules.explanation: The sshd LogLevel setting controls the detail of authentication and session events written to logs (commonly VERBOSE or INFO).
rules.impact: Insufficient SSH logging reduces visibility into brute-force attempts, unusual logins, and other remote-access incidents.

rules.title: SSH MAC algorithms are configured
rules.explanation: SSH MAC algorithms protect the integrity of encrypted SSH packets so tampering can be detected.
rules.impact: Weak MAC algorithms increase the risk that intercepted SSH packets can be modified without detection.

rules.title: SSH MaxAuthTries is configured
rules.explanation: MaxAuthTries limits the number of authentication attempts permitted per SSH connection.
rules.impact: Unlimited authentication tries within a single connection make password guessing more efficient and harder to throttle.

rules.title: SSH MaxSessions is configured
rules.explanation: MaxSessions limits the number of multiplexed sessions that may be opened over a single SSH connection.
rules.impact: Unlimited session multiplexing can enable resource abuse and make auditing of concurrent remote activity more difficult.

rules.title: SSH MaxStartups is configured
rules.explanation: MaxStartups limits concurrent unauthenticated SSH connections, protecting the daemon from connection floods before authentication completes.
rules.impact: Without MaxStartups limits, attackers can exhaust SSH connection capacity and deny remote administrative access.

rules.title: SSH PermitEmptyPasswords is disabled
rules.explanation: PermitEmptyPasswords controls whether accounts with empty password strings may authenticate over SSH.
rules.impact: Allowing empty passwords permits unauthenticated SSH access to accounts that have no password set, which is a critical exposure.

rules.title: SSH PermitRootLogin is disabled
rules.explanation: PermitRootLogin controls whether the root account may authenticate directly over SSH. Administrative access is preferably obtained via individual accounts and privilege elevation.
rules.impact: Direct root SSH login means a single successful credential or key compromise yields immediate unrestricted control and weakens accountability.

rules.title: SSH PermitUserEnvironment is disabled
rules.explanation: PermitUserEnvironment allows users to set environment variables through files such as ~/.ssh/environment that sshd will apply at login.
rules.impact: User-controlled SSH environment settings can alter PATH, library loading, and other variables in ways that bypass intended security controls.

rules.title: SSH UsePAM is enabled
rules.explanation: UsePAM causes sshd to authenticate and establish sessions through the PAM stack, integrating password policy, account locks, and related controls.
rules.impact: Disabling UsePAM bypasses PAM-based password policy, lockout, and multifactor controls for SSH authentication.

rules.title: Sudo is installed
rules.explanation: sudo is the standard mechanism for controlled privilege elevation, allowing authorized users to run specific commands as another user while recording activity.
rules.impact: Without sudo, administrators often share direct root logins, reducing accountability and fine-grained privilege separation.

rules.title: Sudo commands use pty
rules.explanation: The sudo use_pty option forces commands run through sudo to execute in a pseudo-terminal.
rules.impact: Requiring a pty reduces certain classes of abuse involving backgrounded or redirected privileged processes after a sudo invocation.

rules.title: Sudo log file is configured
rules.explanation: sudo can write a dedicated logfile of privileged command invocations, including the invoking user, command, and timing information.
rules.impact: Dedicated sudo logging improves accountability for privileged actions and supports investigation of misuse or compromise.

rules.title: Users must provide a password for privilege escalation
rules.explanation: sudoers NOPASSWD tags allow privileged commands without re-entering a password. Restricting NOPASSWD preserves identity confirmation for elevation.
rules.impact: Passwordless sudo means compromise of an interactive user session immediately yields elevated privileges without an additional authentication barrier.

rules.title: Re-authentication for privilege escalation is not disabled globally
rules.explanation: A global !authenticate tag in sudoers disables authentication requirements for sudo across affected users.
rules.impact: Globally disabling sudo authentication removes a primary control preventing unauthorized privilege elevation from any user session.

rules.title: Sudo authentication timeout is configured
rules.explanation: timestamp_timeout controls how long a successful sudo authentication remains cached before re-authentication is required.
rules.impact: An excessively long or infinite sudo ticket window increases the chance that an unattended authenticated terminal can be abused for privileged commands.

rules.title: A current PAM package is installed
rules.explanation: PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) provides the framework for authentication, account, session, and password management on Linux. Current PAM packages include security fixes and supported modules.
rules.impact: Outdated PAM components may contain known vulnerabilities in a central authentication path used by login, SSH, sudo, and related services.

rules.title: Libpam-modules is installed
rules.explanation: libpam-modules provides commonly used PAM modules such as pam_unix, pam_limits, and pam_env that implement standard authentication and session behavior.
rules.impact: Missing standard PAM modules can break authentication stacks or force insecure fallback configurations.

rules.title: Libpam-pwquality is installed
rules.explanation: libpam-pwquality provides the pam_pwquality module used to enforce password strength requirements during password changes.
rules.impact: Without pam_pwquality packages, password complexity policy cannot be enforced consistently through PAM.

rules.title: The pam_unix module is enabled
rules.explanation: pam_unix performs traditional Unix authentication and password updates against local account databases such as /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow.
rules.impact: Absence of pam_unix from the PAM stack can break local password authentication or force reliance on incomplete alternate mechanisms.

rules.title: The pam_faillock module is enabled
rules.explanation: pam_faillock locks accounts after a configured number of consecutive failed authentication attempts and is commonly used to mitigate password guessing.
rules.impact: Without faillock in the PAM stack, failed logon attempts may be unlimited across console, su, and other PAM-aware services.

rules.title: The pam_pwquality module is enabled
rules.explanation: pam_pwquality evaluates new passwords against quality rules defined in configuration such as /etc/security/pwquality.conf.
rules.impact: Without pam_pwquality in the password stack, users may set weak passwords that are easier to guess or crack.

rules.title: The pam_pwhistory module is enabled
rules.explanation: pam_pwhistory remembers previous passwords and rejects reuse of recent passwords during password changes.
rules.impact: Without password history controls, users can immediately revert to prior passwords, undermining rotation policy.

rules.title: Lockout after failed password attempts is configured
rules.explanation: The deny setting in faillock configuration defines how many consecutive failed authentications trigger an account lock.
rules.impact: Appropriate lockout thresholds slow online password-guessing attacks against local authentication services.

rules.title: Password unlock time is configured
rules.explanation: The unlock_time setting defines how long an account remains locked after exceeding the failed-attempt threshold.
rules.impact: Sufficient unlock delays make repeated online guessing impractical while still allowing eventual recovery of legitimate accounts.

rules.title: Failed password lockout is configured for root
rules.explanation: even_deny_root extends faillock lockout behavior to the root account so root is not exempt from failed-attempt limits.
rules.impact: Exempting root from lockout leaves the most privileged local account continuously exposed to password-guessing attacks.

rules.title: The minimum number of password character changes is configured
rules.explanation: The difok setting requires a minimum number of characters in a new password to differ from the previous password.
rules.impact: Requiring meaningful character changes prevents trivial password updates that satisfy rotation policy without improving strength.

rules.title: Minimum password length is configured
rules.explanation: Minimum password length requirements ensure newly set passwords contain enough characters to provide adequate entropy against guessing attacks.
rules.impact: Short passwords are substantially easier to brute-force. Enforcing sufficient length is a primary control for password strength.

rules.title: The maximum number of repeated characters is configured
rules.explanation: The maxrepeat setting limits how many identical consecutive characters are allowed in a new password.
rules.impact: Restricting repeated characters reduces use of trivial patterns that weaken otherwise policy-compliant passwords.

rules.title: The maximum sequential character length is configured
rules.explanation: The maxsequence setting limits consecutive sequential characters (such as abc or 123) allowed in a new password.
rules.impact: Limiting keyboard and numeric sequences reduces predictable password patterns commonly found in attack dictionaries.

rules.title: Password dictionary checking is enabled
rules.explanation: Dictionary checking compares candidate passwords against lists of common or compromised passwords before accepting a change.
rules.impact: Rejecting dictionary passwords reduces use of credentials that are among the first tried in guessing and credential-stuffing attacks.

rules.title: Password quality checking is enforced
rules.explanation: Enforcement options for pam_pwquality require password quality checks to be applied rather than treated as optional warnings.
rules.impact: Without enforcement, users may bypass quality warnings and continue using weak passwords.

rules.title: Password quality checking is enforced for the root user
rules.explanation: By default some password-quality checks may not apply to root. enforce_for_root extends quality requirements to the root account.
rules.impact: A weak root password is a high-impact exposure. Enforcing quality checks for root reduces that risk.

rules.title: Password history remembering is configured
rules.explanation: The remember setting for pam_pwhistory defines how many previous passwords are retained and rejected on reuse.
rules.impact: Remembering sufficient password history prevents cyclic reuse of the same passwords across forced rotations.

rules.title: Password history is enforced for the root user
rules.explanation: enforce_for_root for pam_pwhistory applies password-history restrictions to the root account as well as ordinary users.
rules.impact: Without history enforcement for root, administrators can immediately reuse prior root passwords after a required change.

rules.title: Pam_pwhistory includes use_authtok
rules.explanation: The use_authtok option tells pam_pwhistory to use the password token already obtained earlier in the PAM stack rather than prompting again.
rules.impact: Consistent token handling across PAM modules avoids conflicting prompts and helps ensure history checks apply to the same password being set.

rules.title: Pam_unix does not include nullok
rules.explanation: The nullok option in pam_unix permits authentication for accounts that have an empty password field.
rules.impact: nullok allows passwordless login for accounts without passwords, which is a critical authentication weakness.

rules.title: Pam_unix does not include remember
rules.explanation: The remember option in pam_unix is a legacy password-history mechanism superseded by pam_pwhistory.
rules.impact: Using remember in pam_unix alongside pam_pwhistory can create conflicting history behavior and unpredictable policy enforcement.

rules.title: Pam_unix uses a strong password hashing algorithm
rules.explanation: pam_unix hashing options select algorithms such as yescrypt, SHA-512, or bcrypt for storing local password hashes.
rules.impact: Weak hashes (such as MD5-based schemes) can be cracked quickly if /etc/shadow is disclosed, exposing user credentials.

rules.title: Pam_unix includes use_authtok
rules.explanation: The use_authtok option tells pam_unix to use the password token already provided earlier in the PAM stack during password updates.
rules.impact: Consistent token use across the password stack helps ensure hashing and related checks operate on the intended new password.

rules.title: Password expiration is configured
rules.explanation: PASS_MAX_DAYS in /etc/login.defs sets the maximum lifetime of a password before it must be changed.
rules.impact: Unbounded password lifetime allows compromised credentials to remain valid indefinitely without forced rotation.

rules.title: Password expiration warning days are configured
rules.explanation: PASS_WARN_AGE in /etc/login.defs defines how many days before expiration users are warned to change their passwords.
rules.impact: Adequate warning reduces abrupt lockouts and unsafe ad-hoc recovery practices when passwords expire unexpectedly.

rules.title: A strong password hashing algorithm is configured
rules.explanation: ENCRYPT_METHOD in /etc/login.defs selects the default hashing algorithm used when new local passwords are created.
rules.impact: Strong hashing algorithms increase the cost of offline cracking if password hashes are obtained from the system.

rules.title: Inactive password lock is configured
rules.explanation: INACTIVE in /etc/login.defs defines how many days after password expiration an account is locked if the password is not changed.
rules.impact: Locking inactive expired accounts reduces the risk that abandoned credentials remain usable after expiration.

rules.title: Last password change date is in the past for all users
rules.explanation: The last password change date recorded for each account should not be set in the future, which would delay normal aging controls.
rules.impact: Future-dated password change values can indicate tampering intended to bypass forced password expiration.

rules.title: Root is the only UID 0 account
rules.explanation: UID 0 confers unrestricted superuser privileges. Only the root account should have UID 0.
rules.impact: Additional UID 0 accounts provide equivalent root access that can bypass monitoring focused on the root username.

rules.title: Root is the only account with GID 0
rules.explanation: Primary group GID 0 is associated with the root group. Ordinary user accounts should not use GID 0 as their primary group.
rules.impact: Accounts with primary GID 0 inherit root-group privileges and can indicate misconfiguration or unauthorized privileged access.

rules.title: Root is the only group with GID 0
rules.explanation: Only the root group should be assigned GID 0 in /etc/group. Additional groups with GID 0 share the same group identity.
rules.impact: Extra GID 0 groups grant root-group privileges to their members and can conceal privileged access paths.

rules.title: Access to the root account is controlled
rules.explanation: Direct root login can be restricted by locking the root password or otherwise preventing interactive root authentication, favoring sudo for elevation.
rules.impact: An unlocked root password creates a direct high-value target for guessing attacks and weakens accountability compared with sudo-based elevation.

rules.title: Root PATH integrity is configured
rules.explanation: The root user's PATH should omit the current directory and empty entries, and directories on PATH should be securely owned and not writable by unprivileged users.
rules.impact: An insecure root PATH can cause execution of attacker-controlled binaries placed in writable directories ahead of system commands.

rules.title: Root user umask is configured
rules.explanation: The umask determines default permission bits removed when the root user creates new files and directories.
rules.impact: An overly permissive root umask can create world- or group-accessible sensitive files by default, increasing accidental exposure.

rules.title: System accounts do not have a valid login shell
rules.explanation: System accounts are intended to run services rather than interactive logins and should use non-login shells such as /usr/sbin/nologin or /bin/false.
rules.impact: Valid login shells on system accounts expand the impact of credential compromise for service identities.

rules.title: Accounts without a valid login shell are locked
rules.explanation: Accounts assigned a non-login shell should also have locked passwords so authentication cannot succeed through alternate PAM entry points.
rules.impact: An unlocked password on a non-login account can still allow authentication via some services if the shell restriction is bypassed or ignored.

rules.title: Nologin is not listed in /etc/shells
rules.explanation: /etc/shells lists valid interactive login shells. Non-login shells such as nologin should not appear in that list.
rules.impact: Listing nologin in /etc/shells can cause some services to treat nologin accounts as having an acceptable shell, contrary to their intended lockout.

rules.title: Default user shell timeout is configured
rules.explanation: The TMOUT setting defines an idle timeout after which interactive shells automatically exit.
rules.impact: Idle shell timeouts reduce the window during which an unattended terminal session can be abused without re-authentication.

rules.title: Default user umask is configured
rules.explanation: A default umask in global shell profiles sets creation permissions for files and directories created by interactive users.
rules.impact: A permissive default umask (such as 022) creates world-readable files by default, increasing the chance of accidental data exposure.

rules.title: The journald service is enabled and active
rules.explanation: systemd-journald collects and stores system journal logs, including service, kernel, and authentication-related events on Ubuntu systems.
rules.impact: Without an active journald service, important security and operational events may not be recorded for detection and investigation.

rules.title: Only one logging system is in use
rules.explanation: Hosts may use journald, rsyslog, or a coordinated combination. Concurrent uncoordinated logging systems can duplicate or omit events.
rules.impact: Conflicting logging configurations create blind spots and complicate correlation during incident response.

rules.title: Systemd-journal-remote is installed
rules.explanation: systemd-journal-remote provides components for receiving or transferring journal logs in centralized logging architectures.
rules.impact: Centralized journal transfer helps preserve log integrity if a host is compromised and local logs are altered or deleted.

rules.title: Systemd-journal-upload is enabled and active
rules.explanation: systemd-journal-upload forwards local journal entries to a remote journal collector for centralized retention and analysis.
rules.impact: Without active upload, security events remain only on the local host and can be destroyed if that host is compromised.

rules.title: The systemd-journal-remote service is not in use
rules.explanation: systemd-journal-remote can accept journal data from remote hosts. Hosts that are not designated log collectors should not expose this service.
rules.impact: An unintended journal intake service expands network attack surface and may allow injection of forged log records.

rules.title: Journald ForwardToSyslog is disabled
rules.explanation: ForwardToSyslog controls whether journald forwards events to traditional syslog. When journald is the sole logging system, forwarding is typically disabled.
rules.impact: Unnecessary ForwardToSyslog can duplicate events and increase noise when a separate syslog daemon is not part of the intended design.

rules.title: Journald compression is configured
rules.explanation: journald can compress stored journal data to reduce disk usage while retaining more history within available space.
rules.impact: Compression helps sustain longer retention for retrospective investigation when disk capacity is limited.

rules.title: Journald persistent storage is configured
rules.explanation: Storage=persistent causes journald to write journals under /var/log/journal on disk rather than keeping them only in volatile storage.
rules.impact: Without persistent storage, journal history is lost on reboot, including events that preceded a crash or forced restart.

rules.title: Rsyslog is installed
rules.explanation: rsyslog is a syslog implementation that filters, formats, and can forward logs to local files or remote collectors.
rules.impact: When rsyslog is the chosen logging system, it must be installed so system and security events can be collected and forwarded as designed.

rules.title: The rsyslog service is enabled and active
rules.explanation: When rsyslog is used, the service should be enabled at boot and actively running so log collection continues across restarts.
rules.impact: A stopped rsyslog daemon interrupts collection of authentication failures, service errors, and other security-relevant events.

rules.title: Journald is configured to send logs to rsyslog
rules.explanation: ForwardToSyslog=yes causes journald to pass events to rsyslog so systemd and kernel messages are included in syslog processing pipelines.
rules.impact: Without forwarding, journal-only events may never reach rsyslog-based SIEM or remote collectors, creating incomplete security visibility.

rules.title: Rsyslog log file creation mode is configured
rules.explanation: rsyslog FileCreateMode (for example 0640) sets default permissions on newly created log files so they are not world-readable.
rules.impact: Overly permissive log file modes allow unprivileged users to read authentication and administrative activity that aids further attacks.

rules.title: Rsyslog is not configured to receive remote logs
rules.explanation: rsyslog input modules such as imtcp and imudp can accept logs from remote clients. Non-collector hosts should not enable remote intake.
rules.impact: Remote log reception opens network listeners that can be abused for forged log injection or denial-of-service through log flooding.

rules.title: Access to all log files is configured
rules.explanation: Files under /var/log should use restrictive modes and ownership so unprivileged users cannot read or alter sensitive log content.
rules.impact: World-readable logs can disclose usernames, timestamps, errors, and other details useful for reconnaissance and privilege escalation.

rules.title: Auditd packages are installed
rules.explanation: auditd is the userspace component of the Linux Audit subsystem, which records security-relevant events based on kernel audit rules.
rules.impact: Without audit packages, kernel-level security event collection required for many compliance and investigation use cases is unavailable.

rules.title: The auditd service is enabled and active
rules.explanation: The auditd service must be enabled and running so audit rules remain loaded and events are written continuously.
rules.impact: A stopped auditd daemon leaves the system without active audit logging of privileged and security-relevant activity.

rules.title: Auditing for processes that start before auditd is enabled
rules.explanation: The kernel audit=1 parameter enables auditing early in boot so events that occur before auditd starts can still be captured.
rules.impact: Without early audit enablement, initialization activity may go unrecorded, reducing visibility into pre-auditd compromise techniques.

rules.title: The audit backlog limit is sufficient
rules.explanation: audit_backlog_limit sizes the kernel queue that holds audit events awaiting delivery to userspace.
rules.impact: An undersized backlog can drop events under load, allowing attackers to obscure activity by overwhelming the audit queue.

rules.title: Audit log storage size is configured
rules.explanation: max_log_file sets the maximum size of individual audit log files before rotation or other configured actions occur.
