rules.impact: Appropriate log size settings help balance retention needs against the risk of filling the audit filesystem.

rules.title: Audit logs are not automatically deleted
rules.explanation: max_log_file_action settings such as keep_logs retain old audit logs rather than deleting them automatically when size limits are reached.
rules.impact: Automatic deletion of audit logs can destroy evidence needed for investigations and compliance retention.

rules.title: The system shuts down when audit logs are full
rules.explanation: auditd can be configured to halt or enter single-user mode when the audit log filesystem has no free space, failing closed rather than continuing unaudited.
rules.impact: In high-security environments, continuing without space for audit records risks undetected unauthorized activity; availability is intentionally subordinated to audit integrity.

rules.title: The system warns when audit log space is low
rules.explanation: space_left_action can notify administrators when free space on the audit partition approaches a configured threshold.
rules.impact: Early warning provides time to free space or rotate archives before auditing stops or the system takes a full-disk action.

rules.title: Changes to the sudoers scope are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules should record modifications to /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d, which define privileged command authorization.
rules.impact: Unaudited sudoers changes can silently expand privileges or introduce NOPASSWD rules that weaken elevation controls.

rules.title: Actions as another user are always logged
rules.explanation: Audit rules that watch identity-changing executions record commands run after switching users through mechanisms such as sudo or su.
rules.impact: Without identity-change auditing, privileged actions may lack attribution needed to determine who executed commands after elevation.

rules.title: Sudo log file changes are collected
rules.explanation: Audit monitoring of the sudo logfile detects modification or truncation that may indicate tampering with privileged-command history.
rules.impact: Attackers with elevated access may alter sudo logs to hide activity; auditing those files helps detect such tampering.

rules.title: Date and time change events are collected
rules.explanation: System calls that adjust the system clock (such as adjtimex, settimeofday, and clock_settime) should be audited.
rules.impact: Unauthorized time changes can disrupt log correlation and create misleading timelines during incident investigation.

rules.title: Use of privileged commands is collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules should record execution of setuid and setgid programs, which can elevate effective privileges when invoked.
rules.impact: Unaudited use of privileged commands reduces visibility into privilege-escalation activity on the host.

rules.title: Unsuccessful file access attempts are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules can record failed open and similar attempts that return permission errors such as EACCES or EPERM.
rules.impact: Patterns of failed file access often indicate reconnaissance or attempts to reach protected data and should be visible to investigators.

rules.title: User and group information changes are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules should record changes to account databases such as /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group, and /etc/gshadow.
rules.impact: Unaudited account database edits can conceal creation of backdoor accounts or unauthorized privilege changes.

rules.title: Successful filesystem mounts are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules should record successful mount operations that attach local or remote filesystems to the directory tree.
rules.impact: Unaudited mounts can conceal attachment of removable media or network shares used for data theft or malware introduction.

rules.title: Session initiation information is collected
rules.explanation: Audit monitoring of session databases such as utmp, wtmp, and btmp records login session creation and related state.
rules.impact: Session records are key investigation artifacts; auditing them helps detect tampering intended to hide interactive access.

rules.title: Login and logout events are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules related to faillog, lastlog, and similar login accounting help capture successful and failed authentication activity.
rules.impact: Without login-event auditing, unauthorized access and password-guessing patterns are harder to detect and reconstruct.

rules.title: File deletion events by users are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules can record unlink, rename, and related system calls used to delete or rename files.
rules.impact: Mass deletion or renaming may indicate anti-forensics, ransomware, or intentional data destruction and should leave an audit trail.

rules.title: Kernel module load and unload events are collected
rules.explanation: System calls such as init_module, finit_module, and delete_module load or remove kernel modules and should be audited.
rules.impact: Unaudited module operations reduce the chance of detecting rootkit-style kernel implants or unauthorized module changes.

rules.title: The audit configuration is immutable
rules.explanation: Setting the audit enabled flag to immutable (-e 2) prevents audit rule changes until the next reboot.
rules.impact: Immutability limits the ability of an attacker with elevated privileges to disable or weaken auditing before further malicious actions.

rules.title: Audit log file permissions are configured
rules.explanation: Audit log files should use restrictive modes (commonly 0600) so only authorized privileged accounts can read them.
rules.impact: Readable audit logs can disclose security events and administrative behavior patterns to unprivileged users.

rules.title: Audit log file owner is configured
rules.explanation: Audit log files should be owned by root so unprivileged users cannot alter ownership-based access to those records.
rules.impact: Incorrect ownership can allow unauthorized modification or deletion of audit evidence.

rules.title: Audit log file group owner is configured
rules.explanation: Audit log files should be group-owned by a privileged group (typically root) consistent with organizational access policy.
rules.impact: Overly broad group ownership can expose audit content to users who do not require access for administration or review.

rules.title: Permissions on the audit log directory are configured
rules.explanation: The /var/log/audit directory should use restrictive mode so unauthorized users cannot list or access audit log contents.
rules.impact: A traversable audit directory can leak metadata even when individual files are mode-restricted, and may enable unauthorized access.

rules.title: Permissions on audit configuration files are configured
rules.explanation: Audit configuration and rules files under /etc/audit control what is logged. Restrictive modes limit unauthorized reading and modification.
rules.impact: Writable audit configuration allows attackers to remove monitoring of their actions and create blind spots in the audit trail.

rules.title: Audit configuration file owner is configured
rules.explanation: Audit configuration files should be owned by root so only privileged administrators can change audit policy.
rules.impact: Incorrect ownership of audit configuration enables unauthorized users to weaken or disable auditing.

rules.title: Audit configuration file group owner is configured
rules.explanation: Audit configuration files should be group-owned by a privileged group (typically root) aligned with who may administer audit policy.
rules.impact: Broad group ownership of audit configuration can allow unauthorized policy changes that hide privileged activity.

rules.title: Permissions on audit tools are configured
rules.explanation: Audit utilities such as auditctl, ausearch, and aureport should have restrictive modes that prevent unauthorized modification.
rules.impact: Writable audit tools can be replaced with trojaned binaries that ignore administrative commands or return false results.

rules.title: Audit tools owner is configured
rules.explanation: Audit administrative utilities should be owned by root so unprivileged users cannot replace them.
rules.impact: Incorrect ownership of audit tools enables substitution attacks that undermine administrators' ability to manage or review auditing.

rules.title: Audit tools group owner is configured
rules.explanation: Audit utilities should be group-owned by a privileged group (typically root) consistent with least-privilege administration.
rules.impact: Broad group write access to audit tools increases the risk of tampering that conceals attacker activity from operators.

rules.title: AIDE is installed
rules.explanation: AIDE (Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment) builds a database of file attributes and hashes to detect unauthorized filesystem changes.
rules.impact: Without integrity monitoring, unauthorized changes to system binaries and configuration may go unnoticed after compromise.

rules.title: Filesystem integrity is checked regularly
rules.explanation: AIDE should run on a recurring schedule (cron or systemd timer) so filesystem integrity deviations are detected promptly.
rules.impact: Infrequent or only manual AIDE runs leave long windows during which unauthorized file changes can remain undetected.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/passwd are configured
rules.explanation: /etc/passwd lists local user accounts and must remain world-readable for normal system operation while writable only by root.
rules.impact: Unauthorized write access to /etc/passwd can create privileged accounts or alter user attributes used for access control.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/passwd- are configured
rules.explanation: /etc/passwd- is a backup of /etc/passwd and should have ownership and mode protections comparable to the primary file.
rules.impact: Weak permissions on passwd backups can expose account details or allow unauthorized restoration of altered account data.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/group are configured
rules.explanation: /etc/group defines local groups and membership. It should be world-readable as required for normal operation and writable only by root.
rules.impact: Unauthorized write access to /etc/group can grant users membership in privileged groups without approved account-management processes.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/group- are configured
rules.explanation: /etc/group- is a backup of /etc/group and should be protected with ownership and mode settings comparable to the primary file.
rules.impact: Weak permissions on group backups can expose membership data or support unauthorized restoration of privileged group changes.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/shadow are configured
rules.explanation: /etc/shadow stores local password hashes and related aging fields. It must not be readable by unprivileged users.
rules.impact: Readable shadow hashes enable offline password cracking. Compromise of hashes can lead to full credential exposure.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/shadow- are configured
rules.explanation: /etc/shadow- is a backup of /etc/shadow and contains the same sensitive password hash material as the primary file.
rules.impact: Weak permissions on shadow backups provide an alternate path to obtain password hashes for offline attack.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/gshadow are configured
rules.explanation: /etc/gshadow stores group passwords and administrator lists. Access should be limited to privileged accounts.
rules.impact: Readable gshadow data can disclose group credentials and privileged membership details useful for unauthorized group access.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/gshadow- are configured
rules.explanation: /etc/gshadow- is a backup of /etc/gshadow and should receive protections equivalent to the primary file.
rules.impact: Weak permissions on gshadow backups can expose group secrets even when the primary file is correctly restricted.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/shells are configured
rules.explanation: /etc/shells lists valid login shells consulted by some services when validating account shells.
rules.impact: Unauthorized modification of /etc/shells can mark untrusted interpreters as valid shells and weaken shell-based access restrictions.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/security/opasswd are configured
rules.explanation: /etc/security/opasswd stores hashed previous passwords used by password-history mechanisms such as pam_pwhistory.
rules.impact: Readable password-history files expose prior hashes that can reveal password patterns and aid cracking of current credentials.

rules.title: World-writable files and directories are protected
rules.explanation: World-writable filesystem objects can be modified by any local user. Sticky bits on shared directories or remediation of unexpected write bits limit abuse.
rules.impact: Unprotected world-writable files allow any user to overwrite contents, which can lead to privilege abuse or denial of service.

rules.title: No unowned files or directories exist
rules.explanation: Files without a valid owning user or group (orphaned ownership) remain after accounts or groups are removed and UIDs/GIDs are no longer defined.
rules.impact: Orphaned objects may later be inherited by a new account reusing the same UID/GID, unintentionally granting access to residual sensitive data.

rules.title: Accounts in /etc/passwd use shadow passwords
rules.explanation: Local accounts should store an 'x' in the /etc/passwd password field and keep actual hashes in /etc/shadow.
rules.impact: Password hashes in world-readable /etc/passwd are immediately available for offline cracking; shadowing confines hashes to a restricted file.

rules.title: Password fields in /etc/shadow are not empty
rules.explanation: An empty password field in /etc/shadow indicates the account has no password hash set for authentication.
rules.impact: Accounts without passwords may authenticate without credentials under some PAM configurations, enabling unauthorized access.

rules.title: No duplicate UIDs exist
rules.explanation: Each local user account should have a unique UID so file ownership and access decisions map to a single identity.
rules.impact: Duplicate UIDs cause multiple accounts to share the same identity for access control, undermining accountability and isolation.

rules.title: No duplicate GIDs exist
rules.explanation: Each local group should have a unique GID so group-based permissions map to a single group identity.
rules.impact: Duplicate GIDs create ambiguous group rights and can be abused to inherit privileges associated with another group name.

rules.title: No duplicate user names exist
rules.explanation: User names in /etc/passwd should be unique so authentication and auditing consistently refer to one account identity.
rules.impact: Duplicate user names with different UIDs create ambiguity between tools and authentication paths that can bypass intended access policy.

rules.title: No duplicate group names exist
rules.explanation: Group names in /etc/group should be unique so membership and permission checks resolve to a single group identity.
rules.impact: Duplicate group names with different GIDs create ambiguity that can be exploited to obtain unintended group privileges.

rules.title: Local interactive user home directories exist
rules.explanation: Interactive user accounts should have existing home directories configured for their login environment and personal files.
rules.impact: Missing home directories can cause applications to write files in unexpected locations and complicate secure per-user configuration.

rules.title: Access to local interactive user dot files is configured
rules.explanation: User startup and configuration files such as .bashrc, .profile, and SSH client settings should not be writable by other users.
rules.impact: Writable dotfiles allow injection of commands that execute when the user next logs in, enabling lateral movement under that user's privileges.
